sections.title: Article 90 — Introduction: how this Code is set up
sections.plain_explanation: Article 90 is the front door of the Code. It explains why the Code exists, what kinds of installations it covers, what it leaves out, and how its chapters fit together. It also explains the difference between a rule you must follow and background material that only helps you understand a rule.
sections.on_the_job: Start here when a question is really about whether the Code applies at all, who enforces it, or whether a note in the book is a requirement. Most day-to-day wiring questions are answered in Chapters 1 through 7, not in Article 90 itself.
sections.figure_idea: A simple map of the NEC: Chapters 1-4 general, 5 special occupancies, 6 special equipment, 7 special conditions, 8 communications standing apart, 9 tables.
sections.florida_note: Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. NEC 2023 takes effect in Florida with the FBC 9th Edition for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026.

sections.title: Purpose of the Code
sections.plain_explanation:
The point of the Code is to protect people and property from the hazards that come with using electricity. Following it, together with proper maintenance, produces an installation that is largely free from hazard. The Code is not a design manual for beginners, and meeting the Code does not promise the most efficient or most convenient system — it sets the safety floor.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 90.1: Article 90 was reshuffled. 90.1 is now the scope of Article 90 itself, and the old purpose statement moved into 90.2, Use and Application. The purpose statement that used to be 90.1 now sits in 90.2, Use and Application, along with what the code covers and doesn't cover.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: When a plan meets the Code but works poorly, that is a design problem, not proof the Code failed. When a shortcut works but is hazardous, the Code still controls. Build to the safety floor first, then to good design above it.
sections.figure_idea: A house and a small shop side by side under one open Code book — the NEC covers both, and everything electrical inside the property line.

sections.title: Scope — what is covered and what is not
sections.plain_explanation: This section lists the kinds of installations the Code covers, such as premises wiring in buildings, yards, parking areas, and similar locations, and the kinds it does not cover, such as most utility-owned generation and distribution installations, ships, railway rolling stock, and mining equipment. It also covers installations where the Code applies only with special permission from the authority having jurisdiction. Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in a house are handled by the building code, not by this article.
sections.on_the_job: The line that matters most in the field is the utility line: work on the customer side of the service point is generally Code work; the utility's own system generally is not. If a job sits in the not-covered or special-permission area, stop and get the AHJ's position before wiring it.
sections.figure_idea: A one-line sketch of a house service showing the service point, with customer-side wiring shaded as NEC work and utility-side wiring shaded differently.
sections.florida_note: House smoke alarms are FBC-Residential R314 and CO alarms are R315 / F.S. 553.885 — building code, not NEC. Existing items L-094, L-095 and L-096 carry those citations; their subsection details carry UNVERIFIED flags in v1 and are not restated here.

sections.title: How the chapters are arranged
sections.plain_explanation: Chapters 1 through 4 apply broadly to electrical installations. Chapters 5, 6 and 7 cover special places, special equipment and special conditions, and they add to or modify the general chapters. Chapter 8 covers communications systems and stands apart — the general chapters only apply to it where a Chapter 8 rule points back to them. Chapter 9 holds tables used by the rest of the book, and the annexes at the back are explanatory, not requirements.
sections.on_the_job: For a normal house or light-commercial job you live in Chapters 1 to 4. Open Chapter 5, 6 or 7 only when the occupancy or equipment is special, and when you do, read that rule together with the general rule it modifies.
sections.figure_idea: Stacked-blocks diagram: Chapters 1-4 as the base, 5-7 as modifying layers, Chapter 8 as a separate tower, Chapter 9 and annexes as reference shelves.

sections.title: Enforcement and the AHJ
sections.plain_explanation:
The authority having jurisdiction — the AHJ, usually the local building department and its inspectors — enforces the Code and approves equipment and installations. The AHJ can grant special permission where the Code allows it, and can interpret how a rule applies to a local situation. An inspector's reading on your job carries weight that a handbook, an app or a study guide does not.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 90.4: The enforcement section was broken into separate subdivisions, and a new informational note sends readers to Annex H for help setting up an inspection program. The inspector's powers didn't change. 90.4 is now split into lettered subdivisions, so each power is easy to find: interpretations (90.4(B)), alternative methods (90.4(C)), products not yet available (90.4(D)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: If a rule could be read two ways on a real job, ask the AHJ before rough-in, not at inspection. Write down who said what and when. This book is a reference aid; the AHJ and the printed NEC govern.
sections.florida_note: Local amendments and AHJ positions always win over a statewide summary, especially on items where enforcement has varied, such as GFCI protection for outdoor HVAC outlets under 210.8(F).

sections.title: Mandatory rules, permissive rules, and explanatory material
sections.plain_explanation:
Mandatory rules use shall or shall not language — they must be followed. Permissive rules use shall be permitted language — they allow an option, they do not require it. Explanatory material, including Informational Notes, is there to explain or point to other material; a note by itself does not create a requirement you can be failed for, and you cannot use a note to override a rule.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 90.5: When the code mentions another standard without giving an edition year, that reference now means the latest edition of that standard. New in 90.5(C): a reference to another standard with no date means that standard's latest edition.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: When someone cites a note as the reason for a red tag or a change, ask for the rule section behind it. Notes are where good explanations live, but the enforceable requirement is always in the rule text or in another standard the rule points to.

sections.title: Formal interpretations
sections.plain_explanation: Where there is a genuine dispute about what a Code rule means, there is a formal process for getting an official interpretation from NFPA. That process is slow and is meant for real disagreements about the text, not for settling a question on one job. One job's question goes to its AHJ.
sections.on_the_job: You will almost never use this section in the field. Know that it exists so you do not treat a magazine article or a forum post as an official interpretation.

sections.title: Examination of equipment for safety
sections.plain_explanation: This section explains how equipment gets examined for safety, normally by being tested and listed or labeled by a qualified testing laboratory. It is the background for the approval, listing and labeling language used all through Article 110. Equipment the AHJ accepts has normally been through that kind of third-party check.
sections.on_the_job: Look for the listing mark and the label when gear arrives. If a piece of equipment has no mark and no paperwork, raise it before it is installed, not after it is wired.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma standard gear is Siemens (S-02). A listing problem is not solved by a familiar brand name — the specific equipment still has to be listed and used within its listing.
sections.figure_idea: Close-up style drawing of a panel label area with the listing mark, ratings and manufacturer instructions called out.

sections.title: Planning for future expansion
sections.plain_explanation: This section encourages planning an installation so later growth in load does not require tearing the system apart. Allowing room for future circuits and capacity is presented as good practice for convenience and for the life of the installation, not as a hard sizing rule by itself. 90.8(B) covers the number of circuits in enclosures: an enclosure may not be filled beyond the number of circuits it was designed and listed to hold.
sections.on_the_job: Spare panel spaces, an accessible junction point, and a raceway path that can be reused are cheap on rough-in day and expensive later. Where the plan allows, leave the next electrician — often us — a workable path.

sections.title: Units of measurement
sections.plain_explanation: Measurements in the Code are shown with metric values and inch-pound values. Where the two do not match exactly because of rounding or a soft conversion, the section explains which value is treated as the requirement. In United States field work the inch-pound value is the one crews measure with.
sections.on_the_job: Measure in inches and feet as printed in the rule you are using. Do not convert a Code dimension yourself and then argue from your conversion at inspection.

sections.title: Article 100 — Definitions: the words the Code uses
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 100 defines the terms that carry a special meaning inside the Code. When a defined word appears in a rule, it means what Article 100 says it means, even if the everyday meaning is broader or narrower. In the 2020 edition the definitions sit in three parts — general definitions, definitions for installations over 1000 volts, and definitions for hazardous (classified) locations — arranged alphabetically inside each part rather than as numbered sections. This chapter covers the job-critical general terms a Sharma helper meets first; it does not attempt every definition in the article.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 100: All definitions were moved into Article 100 (the .2 sections of each article no longer hold definitions; Article 100 is no longer split into parts). Many terms are new or revised, e.g. Counter (Countertop), Work Surface, Servicing, Short Circuit, Likely to Become Energized, Energy Management System, WSCR/WSAF.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: When an argument turns on a single word — accessible, listed, outlet, service — come back to this article before arguing from everyday speech. A surprising number of inspection fights are really definition fights.
sections.figure_idea: An open dictionary: the terms the whole Code shares, defined once in Article 100 instead of being repeated in every article.

sections.title: Accessible and readily accessible
sections.plain_explanation: Accessible, said of equipment, means a person can get close to it to operate, inspect or maintain it, without being blocked by the building's permanent structure. Accessible, said of a wiring method, means it can be removed or reached without tearing out finished construction. Readily accessible is stricter: a person can get to it quickly, without tools other than a key, without climbing over obstacles, and without a portable ladder.
sections.on_the_job: A breaker behind a locked door the occupant can open is different from a junction box buried behind drywall. Buried boxes are the classic failure: a wiring method that cannot be reached without demolition is not accessible, and splices belong in accessible boxes.
sections.figure_idea: Two panels: one reached by a clear path marked readily accessible, one behind stored shelving and a ladder marked not readily accessible.

sections.title: Ampacity
sections.plain_explanation: Ampacity is the most current, in amperes, a conductor can carry continuously in its actual conditions of use without getting hotter than its temperature rating allows. It is not a single number printed on the wire; it depends on the conductor material, insulation rating, ambient temperature, and how many current-carrying conductors share a raceway or cable.
sections.on_the_job: Start from Table 310.16, then adjust for the job's real conditions. A conductor that is fine alone in a cool space can be over its limit bundled in a hot Florida attic.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: CCA is rated from the aluminum column of Table 310.16, which is why Sharma goes one AWG size larger when CCA is used.
sections.figure_idea: Cross-section of a conductor with heat arrows leaving it: ampacity is set by the heat the insulation can take, not by the copper alone.
sections.florida_note: Florida attic temperatures make ambient correction a real design step, not a paperwork exercise.

sections.title: Conductors — bare, covered, insulated, and the neutral
sections.plain_explanation: Article 100 sorts conductors by what is on the metal. A bare conductor has no covering or insulation at all. A covered conductor has a covering that is not recognized insulation — it may protect against weather or abrasion, but it earns the wire no insulation rating. An insulated conductor has insulation that is recognized for the use, which is the normal building wire a crew handles. The neutral conductor is the conductor connected to the system's neutral point that is intended to carry current under normal conditions; the neutral point is the common point of a wye connection, or the midpoint of a single-phase or DC system, from which the circuit conductors are referenced.
sections.on_the_job: Do not treat a covered conductor as insulated when a rule calls for insulation — service-drop covering is the classic example. And the neutral is a current-carrying working conductor, not a spare ground: it lands on the neutral bar and is only bonded to ground where the Code allows the bond.
sections.figure_idea: Three wire cross-sections side by side: bare metal, a weather covering, and full insulation, with the neutral point of a wye drawn beside them.

sections.title: Voltage — nominal voltage, voltage to ground, and circuit voltage
sections.plain_explanation: Three voltage terms run through the whole Code. Voltage of a circuit is the greatest difference of potential between any two conductors of that circuit. Nominal voltage is the value the system is named by — 120, 240, 480 — used to classify circuits and equipment even though the actual voltage wanders a little above and below it. Voltage to ground is the voltage between a conductor and the earth or the grounded point of the system: on a 120/240V house service it is 120V, and on a 208Y/120V system it is 120V, which is why so many clearance and working-space rules key on it instead of the phase-to-phase number.
sections.on_the_job: When a table asks for voltage to ground, answer with the leg-to-ground number, not the nameplate of the service. A 120/240V panel sits in the 0–150V-to-ground row even though 240V appears across its bus.
sections.figure_idea: A 120/240V panel diagram with 120V arrows from each leg to ground and a 240V arrow leg-to-leg, each labelled with its term.

sections.title: Appliance
sections.plain_explanation: An appliance is utilization equipment, usually built as a unit, that does a household or similar job — cooking, washing, drying, comfort heating or cooling, and the like — other than a basic luminaire or motor by itself. The word matters because several branch-circuit and disconnect rules turn on whether the load is an appliance.
sections.on_the_job: Dishwashers, disposals, ranges, dryers and built-in microwaves are appliances. When a rule says appliance, check whether the equipment in front of you fits that idea before applying a general receptacle rule to it.
sections.sharma_note: S-06 is PENDING. The microwave gets its own 20A circuit. The wire is not settled — 12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA — until Mike Holt rules. If the plan or the nameplate states a size, that statement governs.

sections.title: Approved, identified, labeled, and listed
sections.plain_explanation: These four words form one family. Approved means acceptable to the AHJ. Identified means recognizable as suitable for the specific use in question. Labeled means a testing organization has attached its label after checking samples of the product. Listed means the product appears in that organization's published list of items it has evaluated. A product can be well made and still not be listed, and an unlisted product used where listing is required is a Code problem.
sections.on_the_job: Read the box and the device. Breakers must be listed and identified for the panel they go in; a breaker that physically fits a foreign panel is not thereby identified for it.
sections.sharma_note: S-02: all new gear is Siemens. S-03: in an existing Square D panel, use Square D breakers listed for that panel — never mix brands to fill a space.
sections.figure_idea: Four stacked badges showing the chain: tested by a lab, listed in its directory, labeled on the product, approved by the AHJ for the job.

sections.title: Equipment, utilization equipment, enclosures, and fittings
sections.plain_explanation: Equipment is the Code's umbrella word for the apparatus of an installation — fittings, devices, appliances, luminaires, machines and the like, whether they carry current or just support the parts that do. Utilization equipment is the narrower slice that actually uses electric energy to do work: heating, lighting, cooling, data processing and similar jobs. An enclosure is the case or housing around apparatus that keeps people away from live parts and protects the contents; enclosed describes apparatus that has such a case. A fitting is an accessory — a locknut, bushing or similar part — that does a mechanical job rather than an electrical one. A handhole enclosure is a small below-grade access enclosure, set flush or buried, whose cover a worker removes by hand to reach the conductors inside.
sections.on_the_job: Calling something 'equipment' is what brings the Article 110 rules with it — approval, working space, guarding. Handholes are the buried splice points on site work: they are enclosures, so the splices inside still have to be made with listed methods and the cover kept accessible, not paved over.
sections.figure_idea: A panel, a luminaire and a handhole in grade, each tagged with the term that covers it.

sections.title: Bonding — bonded, bonding conductor, bonding jumper
sections.plain_explanation: Bonding means joining metal parts together so they stay at the same electrical potential and have a reliable, low-impedance path that can carry fault current. A bonding jumper is the conductor or fitting that makes that connection. Bonding is not the same job as grounding to the earth; its main safety job is to make fault current flow hard enough to trip the breaker fast.
sections.on_the_job: Metal boxes, raceways, enclosures and equipment frames that can become energized need a bonding path back to the source. A loose locknut or paint under a fitting can quietly break that path.
sections.figure_idea: A metal box and raceway with the fault-current path highlighted returning to the panel, separate from the ground rod path to earth.

sections.title: Grounding conductors and electrodes — EGC, GEC, and bonding jumpers
sections.plain_explanation: The grounding family splits by job. The equipment grounding conductor (EGC) connects the metal frames of equipment back to the source so a ground fault becomes a big fault current that trips the breaker — it is usually the green or bare wire, but 250.118 also lets certain raceways and cable armor serve as the EGC.. The grounding electrode conductor (GEC) connects the system to the grounding electrode — the rod, plate, concrete-encased electrode or other recognized earth connection itself. The main bonding jumper is the connection at the service between the grounded conductor and the EGC side; a system bonding jumper does the same job at a separately derived system. The existing Bonding and Grounded/Grounding pages cover the base words; this page is the conductor-by-conductor map.
sections.on_the_job: Mixing up the EGC and the GEC is the classic exam and inspection trap: the EGC protects people from energized metal, the GEC connects the system to earth, and they are sized from different tables (250.122 for the EGC, 250.66 for the GEC). In a normal house the only neutral-to-ground bond is the main bonding jumper at the service; a separately derived system (for example a transformer or a generator switched as an SDS) gets its own system bonding jumper, and downstream panels keep neutral and ground separate. — downstream panels keep them separate.
sections.figure_idea: A house service diagram tracing three paths in three colours: EGC back to the panel, GEC down to the rod, and the main bonding jumper tying neutral to the enclosure at the service only.

sections.title: Grounded and grounding — telling the conductors apart
sections.plain_explanation: Grounded means connected to the earth, or to a body that serves in place of the earth. The grounded conductor is the system conductor that is intentionally grounded — in a house, the neutral. The grounding conductor, including the equipment grounding conductor, is the path that ties equipment and enclosures to the grounding system for fault protection. The two words differ by one syllable and do completely different jobs, which is why the Code defines them separately.
sections.on_the_job: White is the grounded conductor; green or bare is the grounding conductor. They are bonded together only where the Code permits — at the service — and kept separate downstream in the panels Sharma sets.
sections.figure_idea: Panel detail with the neutral bar and ground bar labelled grounded vs grounding, and the single bonding point at the service marked.

sections.title: Ground fault, GFCI, and ground-fault protection of equipment
sections.plain_explanation: A ground fault is an unintended connection between an ungrounded conductor and normally non-current-carrying metal or the earth — the fault the EGC exists to turn into a breaker trip. Two protective terms build on it and are not interchangeable. A ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protects people: it watches for current leaking outside the intended path and opens the circuit at a few milliamperes, the personnel-protection level (a Class A GFCI must trip when ground-fault current reaches 6 mA and must not trip below 4 mA — Art. 100 GFCI Informational Note, from UL 943).. Ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) protects equipment and conductors from damaging fault currents at much higher levels — hundreds of amperes on large services — and is not intended to protect a person from shock.
sections.on_the_job: A GFPE breaker on a big service will not save a helper who contacts a live part, and a receptacle GFCI is not equipment protection for a service. When a spec or an inspector says 'ground-fault protection,' ask which of the two is meant before ordering gear.
sections.figure_idea: Two trip curves side by side: a GFCI opening at a few milliamperes for personnel, and GFPE opening at hundreds of amperes for equipment.

sections.title: Branch circuit
sections.plain_explanation: A branch circuit is the part of the wiring system between the final overcurrent device protecting it — the breaker in the panel — and the outlets it feeds. Everything upstream of that breaker is a feeder or service conductor; everything downstream to the receptacles, lights and equipment is the branch circuit. Article 210 builds its rules on this definition.
sections.on_the_job: When you size, protect or troubleshoot a circuit, find its breaker first. The conductor size, the breaker rating and the outlets all have to agree as one branch circuit.
sections.sharma_note: S-01: on commercial work every branch circuit is 20A minimum on 12 AWG copper minimum — no 15A branch circuits on commercial jobs. That is Sharma practice, stricter than the Code floor.
sections.figure_idea: One-line diagram: a breaker in the panel and the run out to the outlets it feeds, shaded as the branch circuit.

sections.title: Branch-circuit types — appliance, general purpose, individual, multiwire
sections.plain_explanation: Article 100 names four branch-circuit types. An appliance branch circuit feeds energy-utilizing equipment other than luminaires. A general purpose branch circuit feeds two or more receptacles or outlets for lighting and appliances. An individual branch circuit feeds only one piece of utilization equipment. A multiwire branch circuit uses two or more ungrounded conductors that have a voltage between them, sharing one grounded (neutral) conductor that carries only the unbalanced difference between them — the shared-neutral circuit a crew meets on kitchen and homerun work. The base Branch circuit page covers where a branch circuit starts and ends; this page is the family tree.
sections.on_the_job: The shared neutral is what makes a multiwire circuit efficient and dangerous at the same time: open that neutral under load and the two legs go in series across 240V, over-volting one side. Both legs must disconnect together, and the conductors must land on opposite legs — same-leg 'sharing' overloads the neutral instead of cancelling.
sections.figure_idea: Four simple one-line diagrams, one per type, with the multiwire circuit showing two hots sharing one neutral.

sections.title: Circuit breaker, panelboard, cabinet, and the fault ratings
sections.plain_explanation: A circuit breaker is a device that opens and closes a circuit by nonautomatic means and opens it automatically at a preset overcurrent — an adjustable-trip breaker lets that trip setting be changed without swapping internal parts. A panelboard is a single panel, or group of panel units, of switches or breakers in a cabinet, designed to mount in or against a wall; the enclosure is a cabinet or a cutout box — two separately defined terms (a cabinet has a frame/trim for a swinging door; a cutout box has a door or cover hinged directly to the box walls)., surface or flush, with doors or trim as designed. Two fault ratings live here and are constantly confused: interrupting rating is the highest fault current a device itself can safely open at its rated voltage; short-circuit current rating (SCCR) is the fault current a piece of equipment as a whole can withstand or be protected at. The 110.9 and 110.10 pages carry the rules behind both ratings.
sections.on_the_job: A breaker that fits is not a breaker that belongs: its interrupting rating must meet or beat the available fault current at its terminals, and the panel's SCCR must cover the installation — check the labels before the gear is set, not at inspection.
sections.figure_idea: A panelboard cutaway: breakers inside, cabinet around them, with callouts for the interrupting rating on a breaker label and the SCCR on the panel label.

sections.title: Feeder
sections.plain_explanation: A feeder is the set of circuit conductors between the service equipment, or another power supply source such as a separately derived system, and the final branch-circuit overcurrent devices. It is the middle layer of the system: service conductors feed the service equipment, feeders carry power onward to panels, and branch circuits run from those panels' breakers to the outlets. Rules for sizing, protection and grounding change depending on which layer a conductor belongs to.
sections.on_the_job: The house-to-detached-garage panel run is the everyday feeder: it starts at an overcurrent device in the house panel and ends at the breakers in the garage panel. Call a run by its right layer before applying any sizing or grounding rule to it.
sections.figure_idea: One-line diagram: service equipment feeding a subpanel, the run between them shaded as the feeder and the branch circuits beyond left unshaded.

sections.title: Continuous load
sections.plain_explanation: A continuous load is a load where the maximum current is expected to keep flowing for three hours or more at a stretch. The three-hour line is the whole definition. Continuous loads drive the familiar 125 percent sizing treatment for conductors and overcurrent devices in the articles that use the term.
sections.on_the_job: Lighting in a store that stays on all day, an EV charger, and long-running HVAC loads are the usual suspects. Ask how long the load actually runs before deciding whether the continuous-load treatment applies.
sections.figure_idea: A timeline graphic: a load running 2 hours marked noncontinuous, the same load running 3 hours and beyond marked continuous.

sections.title: Demand factor, nonlinear load, and overcurrent
sections.plain_explanation: Demand factor is the ratio of the maximum demand of a system (or part of one) to the total connected load — it is always 1.0 or less, and it is what lets a feeder be smaller than the sum of everything plugged into it, because not everything runs at once. A nonlinear load is a load whose current waveform does not follow the voltage waveform — LED drivers, electronic ballasts, variable-speed drives and most plug-in electronics — which pushes harmonic current onto the system, especially the shared neutral. Overcurrent is any current above a conductor's or equipment's rating, from either of two causes crews must tell apart: an overload is too much legitimate load in an otherwise sound circuit, while a short circuit or ground fault is a failure — the protection and the troubleshooting are different for each.
sections.on_the_job: Demand factor is why the service math in Chapter 2 never just adds every breaker. Nonlinear loads are why a shared neutral on a multiwire circuit feeding LED lighting may need to be treated as current-carrying and sometimes upsized — the harmonics add on the neutral instead of cancelling.
sections.figure_idea: A bar chart: connected load tall, maximum demand shorter, the ratio labelled demand factor; beside it a distorted current waveform labelled nonlinear.

sections.title: Dwelling unit
sections.plain_explanation: A dwelling unit is a single unit that provides complete and independent living facilities for one or more people, including permanent provisions for living, sleeping, eating, cooking and sanitation. All four functions matter. A space with beds but no cooking or sanitation is not a dwelling unit, and many house rules in the Code switch on or off based on this definition.
sections.on_the_job: One-family houses and each apartment in a multifamily building are dwelling units. A hotel room without permanent cooking provisions generally is not, which changes which receptacle and protection rules apply to it.
sections.figure_idea: Cutaway of one home: living, sleeping, cooking and sanitation together in a single unit behind one front door.

sections.title: Bathroom and clothes closet
sections.plain_explanation: A bathroom, in Article 100, is an area that includes a basin plus one or more of a toilet, a urinal, a tub, a shower, a bidet, or a similar plumbing fixture. — a room with only a toilet and no basin is not a bathroom under the Code, and a basin with nothing else is not either. The definition matters because whole rule sets switch on it: the 20A bathroom receptacle circuit, GFCI protection for bathroom receptacles, and the ban on receptacles inside tub and shower spaces. A clothes closet is the nonhabitable room or space meant for storing clothes — the definition behind the luminaire rules that keep hot, exposed lamps away from stored clothing and shelving.
sections.on_the_job: On plans, check the fixture list before applying bathroom rules: a powder room with a basin and toilet is a bathroom; a water closet alone is not. In closets, the clothes-closet definition is what triggers the luminaire type and clearance rules in 410.16 — treat any closet with a rod and shelf as one unless the plans say otherwise.
sections.figure_idea: Two small floor plans: basin + toilet ticked as a bathroom, toilet alone crossed, with a closet plan showing shelf and rod.

sections.title: Exposed — live parts and wiring methods
sections.plain_explanation: Exposed has two uses. For live parts, it means a part can be accidentally touched or approached nearer than a safe distance — it is not properly guarded, isolated or insulated. For a wiring method, it means the wiring is on or against a surface, or behind panels meant to allow access, rather than permanently hidden inside the building structure.
sections.on_the_job: A cable run on the surface of a garage wall is exposed wiring and needs the protection its article requires. A live bus that a finger can reach is exposed live parts and is a guarding problem under Article 110.

sections.title: Concealed
sections.plain_explanation: Concealed describes wiring or equipment that is made inaccessible by the structure or finish of the building — behind drywall, above a finished ceiling, inside a slab. It is the mirror of the Exposed page: concealed does not mean hidden from the Code. Concealed work still has to be installed by the rules for the method, because once the finish goes on, nobody can inspect or reach it without demolition — which is exactly why rough-in inspection happens before cover.
sections.on_the_job: Anything concealed still has to be accessible where the Code demands access — junction boxes and splices may not be buried behind finish, the trap the Accessible page warns about. If a box will end up concealed and unreachable, move it or add an access panel before the drywall goes up.
sections.figure_idea: A wall cross-section: cable and a box inside the finished wall marked concealed, with the box flagged as the part that may not be buried.

sections.title: Locations — dry, damp, and wet
sections.plain_explanation: A dry location is one not normally damp or wet, though it can be temporarily damp during construction. A damp location is partly protected from weather or subject to moderate moisture — under a canopy, in some basements and barns, and similar places. A wet location is where water or other liquid can contact the equipment directly, or the installation is underground or in concrete or masonry in contact with the earth. The location decides what equipment and wiring methods are suitable.
sections.on_the_job: In Florida, treat exterior work as wet unless it is genuinely sheltered, and slabs and below-grade runs as wet by definition. Use equipment identified for the location you actually have, not the one you wish you had.
sections.figure_idea: Three house vignettes: an interior bedroom marked dry, a covered porch marked damp, an open exterior wall and a slab run marked wet.
sections.florida_note: Florida humidity and wind-driven rain push many borderline porch and carport locations toward damp or wet in the AHJ's judgment. Confirm borderline locations with the inspector rather than assuming dry.

sections.title: Weatherproof, watertight, and dusttight
sections.plain_explanation: Three enclosure-exposure terms, in rising order of sealing. Weatherproof means constructed or protected so that exposure to the weather does not interfere with successful operation — rain may reach it, but the equipment still works; it does not promise that water stays out. Watertight means constructed so moisture does not enter the enclosure under specified test conditions — the seal itself is the point. Dusttight means constructed so dust does not enter under specified test conditions. These sit alongside the Locations page: the location says how wet the place is, these terms say what the enclosure does about its environment.
sections.on_the_job: Weatherproof is the word that fools people — a weatherproof bell box sheds weather well enough to work, but it is not watertight, and neither word substitutes for the wet-location listing and in-use cover rules where those apply. Read the enclosure's actual rating for the job at hand.
sections.figure_idea: Three enclosures in rain: one working with water running off, one sealed against entry, one sealed against dust, each labelled.

sections.title: Outlet and receptacle
sections.plain_explanation: An outlet is any point on the wiring system where current is taken to feed utilization equipment — a receptacle point, a lighting point, a smoke-alarm point and a hardwired equipment connection are all outlets. A receptacle is the contact device installed at an outlet for plugging in a cord-connected load, and a receptacle outlet is an outlet where one or more receptacles are installed. Every receptacle is at an outlet, but not every outlet is a receptacle.
sections.on_the_job: Spacing and circuit rules that say outlet usually count lighting and hardwired points too, while rules that say receptacle outlet count only plug points. Mixing the two up is a common cause of a missed required receptacle or a wrong box-fill count.
sections.sharma_note: S-04: receptacle boxes sit 18 in to the bottom of the box when the plan is silent; when the plan states a height, the plan governs.
sections.figure_idea: A wall elevation with four outlets circled — receptacle, ceiling light, smoke alarm, hardwired dishwasher — and only the first labelled receptacle outlet.

sections.title: Luminaire and lighting outlet
sections.plain_explanation: A luminaire is the complete lighting unit — lamp or LED source, the parts that distribute the light, position and protect the source, and connect it to the supply. It is the Code's word for what crews call a fixture, and the Code uses luminaire everywhere a rule means the whole unit, not just the bulb. A lighting outlet is an outlet intended to connect directly to a luminaire or lampholder — one of the outlet types on the Outlet and receptacle page, and the point where the branch circuit's responsibility for that light ends.
sections.on_the_job: Fixture counts on a takeoff are luminaire counts. When a rule or a plan says 'lighting outlet,' it means the box and circuit point, whether or not the luminaire itself has been set yet — rough-in is inspected against outlets, trim against luminaires.
sections.figure_idea: A ceiling box labelled lighting outlet with the luminaire below it labelled as the complete unit, lamp to housing.

sections.title: Service — the family of service terms
sections.plain_explanation: The service is the conductors and equipment that deliver power from the serving utility to the premises wiring. Service conductors run from the service point to the service disconnect. Service equipment is the gear — normally the disconnect and overcurrent devices — that controls and cuts off the supply. The service point is the handoff line between the utility's system and the premises wiring, and most service rules in Article 230 are built from these definitions.
sections.on_the_job: Find the service point first on any service change. It decides whose rules govern each run of conductor and where the grounded and grounding conductors are bonded together.
sections.sharma_note: S-09: meter outside and panel inside, back to back, where the house allows. The working-space rules of 110.26 still apply in full to that panel.
sections.figure_idea: One-line from utility pole through drop, meter and main disconnect into the panel, with service point, service conductors and service equipment labelled.
sections.florida_note: The utility serving the job (for example FPL or a municipal utility) sets its own service-point and meter requirements alongside the NEC. Confirm the utility's current requirements on service work.

sections.title: Service conductors, drop, lateral, entrance, equipment, and point
sections.plain_explanation: The service family, piece by piece. The service point is the point where the utility's facilities meet the premises wiring — the boundary of responsibility. Service conductors run from the service point to the service disconnecting means. Overhead, they split into the service drop (the utility's overhead conductors from its system to the service point) and service-entrance conductors (on the customer side, from the service point to the service equipment). Underground, the utility's run to the service point is the service lateral. Service equipment is the gear — usually the main disconnect and its enclosure — that controls and cuts off the supply to the building. The base Service page introduces the family; this page is the map of who owns what, where.
sections.on_the_job: Nearly every service argument is a service-point argument: whose conductor, whose repair, whose standard. On Sharma services the meter sits outside and the panel inside, back to back, so the service-entrance run stays as short as the layout allows — and the utility's requirements govern everything on its side of the point.
sections.sharma_note: S-09: meter outside and panel inside, back to back, where the layout allows — the arrangement that keeps the service-entrance conductors short.
sections.figure_idea: An overhead and an underground service side by side, each split at a marked service point: drop/lateral on the utility side, entrance conductors and service equipment on the building side.

sections.title: In sight from — and disconnecting means
sections.plain_explanation: Two linked terms. A disconnecting means is the device, or group of devices, that disconnects a circuit's conductors from their supply — a breaker or a disconnect switch are the everyday examples. Equipment is in sight from other equipment when it is visible from it and not more than 50 ft away; both halves matter, so a disconnect 20 ft away but hidden behind a wall is not in sight. Many equipment articles require a disconnect to be in sight from the equipment it serves, or to be lockable where they allow it to be out of sight.
sections.on_the_job: When you set a condenser or air-handler disconnect, stand at the equipment and look: if you cannot see the disconnect, or it is beyond 50 ft, the in-sight option is not met and the lockable route or a relocation is the conversation to have before trim-out.
sections.figure_idea: A condenser with a sight line drawn to its disconnect on the wall 15 ft away marked in sight, and a second disconnect drawn behind a fence marked not in sight.

sections.title: Device, disconnecting means, and switch types
sections.plain_explanation: A device is a unit of an electrical system, other than a conductor, that carries or controls electric energy — switches, receptacles, breakers and thermostats are devices; wire and conduit are not. A disconnecting means is a device, group of devices, or other means by which the conductors of a circuit can be disconnected from their source — the thing the In Sight page measures from. Three switch types round out the family: a general-use switch controls lighting and appliance loads and is rated in amperes at its marked voltage; an isolating switch is meant to isolate a circuit from its source and is not intended to interrupt current under load; a motor-circuit switch is rated in horsepower and is built to interrupt the maximum operating overload current of the motor it serves.
sections.on_the_job: An isolating switch is not a load-break switch — opening one under load is an arc event, not a disconnect. When a rule calls for a disconnecting means, check that the device in hand is actually rated to do the disconnecting job for that load type.
sections.figure_idea: Three switches in a row — general-use, isolating, motor-circuit — with the load each is built to interrupt drawn beside it.

sections.title: Premises wiring, separately derived systems, raceway, and splices
sections.plain_explanation: The premises wiring system is all the wiring inside (and attached to) a building, from the service point — or from another power source such as a generator or solar system — out to the outlets; it does not include the internal wiring of equipment itself. A separately derived system is a premises wiring system fed from a source other than a service — a transformer, generator, converter or battery — that has no direct electrical connection to the supply conductors of another system, other than through grounding and bonding. A raceway is an enclosed channel built to hold conductors or cables — conduit and tubing are raceways; cable is not. A splice is the connection between conductors, and a splicing wire connector is the device — wire nut, lever connector, terminal block — listed to make that connection under pressure. A hoistway is the shaft-like space an elevator, dumbwaiter or similar equipment travels in, a space with its own wiring rules in Article 620.
sections.on_the_job: A transformer-fed panel is a separately derived system, which is why it gets its own neutral-to-ground bond through a system bonding jumper — the bond the Grounding family page describes. And every splice a crew makes lives or dies by the connector's listing: the connector, not the tape over it, is the splice.
sections.figure_idea: A building outline from service point to last outlet labelled premises wiring, a transformer feeding its own panel labelled separately derived, and a raceway cut open to show the conductors inside.

sections.title: Special permission
sections.plain_explanation: Special permission is the written consent of the AHJ, given where the Code says the AHJ may allow an alternative. It is not a verbal okay from a plans examiner, a builder or a homeowner, and it is not something an electrician grants himself. Where the Code requires it, get it in writing before the work is done.
sections.on_the_job: If a job depends on special permission, paper it: keep the AHJ's written consent with the permit documents so the next inspector sees the same record.

sections.title: Garage, kitchen, and laundry area — how the Code uses area names
sections.plain_explanation: Of these three area names, only one is a formal Article 100 definition: a kitchen is "an area with a sink and permanent provisions for food preparation and cooking" — both halves must be present, and a portable appliance plugged in on the counter does not create one. Garage and laundry area carry no standalone Article 100 definition in the 2020 Code. The Code uses both terms in its rules — garage receptacles and their GFCI protection in 210.8(A)(2) and 210.52(G), the laundry area branch circuit in 210.11(C)(2) and laundry-area GFCI in 210.8(A)(10) — and they take their ordinary meaning: the garage is the vehicle space and its attached unfinished areas, and the laundry area is where laundry equipment is installed or intended to be. So treat the kitchen test as a definition to apply exactly, and the other two as usage terms settled by the plan's intended use of the space.
sections.on_the_job: When a plan is vague about a room's use, settle it before rough-in — a laundry area moved after wiring changes GFCI protection and circuit requirements. The detailed area rules live in Article 210 and are covered in Chapter 2 of this book.
sections.sharma_note: S-08: the dryer circuit uses a Siemens Q230GF 30A 2-pole GFCI breaker, because NEC 2020 requires GFCI protection for receptacles in laundry areas, including 250V receptacles.
sections.figure_idea: House plan with garage, kitchen and laundry shaded in three colors, each tagged with the chapter that carries its main rules.

sections.title: Article 110 — Requirements for electrical installations
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 110 sets the general rules that apply to almost every installation: use approved and listed equipment the way its listing intends, terminate conductors correctly, do neat and workmanlike work, mark what needs marking, and leave safe working space around equipment. If a habit is wrong on every job, the rule against it is probably in this article.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.29: The 50-ft, must-be-visible test for in-sight-from now stands as its own requirement in 110.29 instead of hiding inside an Article 100 definition. In sight now has its own rule, 110.29: the equipment must be visible from the other equipment and 50 ft away or closer.
• 110.33(A): Requirements for access and egress from working space for equipment over 1000 volts, nominal, was revised and clarified in Section 110.33(A)
• 110.34(A): Section 110.34(A) was revised to address the condition of the work surface making up the floor, grade, or platform area within the working space of electrical equipment 1000 volts, nominal, and above.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Most Article 110 failures are visible without a meter: wrong-brand breakers, sloppy terminations, unmarked disconnects, blocked panels. A slow walk with this article in mind catches them before the inspector does.

sections.title: Scope of Article 110
sections.plain_explanation: This short section states that Article 110 covers the general requirements for electrical installations — the approval, installation, ratings, connections, marking and working space of equipment wherever the Code applies. It is not limited to services or to panels; it follows equipment into every occupancy the later articles cover, and the specific articles then add their own rules on top.
sections.on_the_job: When a question is about equipment in general rather than one wiring method — a rating, a marking, a clearance — start in Article 110 before hunting through the equipment's own article.

sections.title: Approval of equipment and conductors
sections.plain_explanation: Conductors and equipment required or permitted by the Code must be approved, which in practice means acceptable to the AHJ. Approval is normally shown through listing and labeling by a qualified testing laboratory. Equipment with no path to approval does not become acceptable because it was cheap, available, or already on the truck.
sections.on_the_job: Check approvals at order and delivery time. A non-listed substitute discovered at trim-out costs a return trip and can hold up the whole job.
sections.sharma_note: S-02 and S-03 keep Sharma inside this rule: Siemens gear for new work, and only breakers listed for the panel in existing panels.

sections.title: Examination, identification, installation, and use of equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
When equipment is examined for approval, the things considered include its suitability for the installation, its mechanical strength, wire-bending space, electrical insulation, heating effects, arcing behavior, and how it is classified by type, size, voltage, current capacity and specific use. In plain terms: the right equipment, of the right rating, in the right place, with room for its conductors to land properly.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.3: Cybersecurity for networked life safety equipment joined the list of things weighed when judging equipment, and gear identified for a use now has to be installed and used by its instructions too. New 110.3(A)(8): approving networked life safety gear now means weighing its cybersecurity, so it holds up against hacking and unauthorized updates and keeps working safely.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Suitability is decided before installation. A device rated for a dry interior wall does not become suitable on an exterior wet wall because it was the one in the box.

nec2023_change.change: Cybersecurity for networked life safety equipment joined the list of things weighed when judging equipment, and gear identified for a use now has to be installed and used by its instructions too. New 110.3(A)(8): approving networked life safety gear now means weighing its cybersecurity, so it holds up against hacking and unauthorized updates and keeps working safely.

sections.title: Install and use listed equipment per its instructions
sections.plain_explanation:
Listed and labeled equipment has to be installed and used following the instructions that come with its listing and labeling. The manufacturer's instructions are not suggestions where the listing depends on them — a torque value, a conductor material, a temperature rating or a mounting requirement in those instructions has Code force through this section.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.3(B): Created a new informational note allowing the use of a QR code to access installation instructions.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: This is the daily rule behind half of field quality: read the label inside the panel door, the sheet in the device box, and the nameplate on the equipment. If the instructions and a habit disagree, the instructions win.
sections.figure_idea: Panel door label enlarged, with torque table, conductor material and temperature rating highlighted as instructions that carry Code force.

nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 110.3(B) Examination, Identification, Installation, Use, and Listing (Product Certification) of Equipment.

sections.title: Voltages
sections.plain_explanation:
The voltage considered is the voltage at which the circuit operates, and equipment's voltage rating may not be less than the nominal voltage of the circuit it is connected to. Equipment is used at the voltage it is rated for, and where the Code states a voltage it means the nominal system voltage the circuit actually operates at, unless a rule says otherwise. A device rated for a lower voltage does not become suitable on a higher-voltage circuit because its terminals fit, and the nominal voltage is what load, protection and clearance rules are keyed to.

Common nominal system voltages (the list itself is in 220.5(A), not 110.4):
• 120 V — single-phase branch circuits
• 120/240 V — the standard one-family house service
• 208Y/120 V — three-phase wye, common in commercial buildings and multifamily services
• 240 V — single-phase or three-phase delta
• 277 V — one leg of a 480Y/277 V system to neutral, the commercial lighting voltage
• 480Y/277 V and 480 V — larger commercial services
Equipment is rated for the nominal voltage of the system it is connected to; a device marked for one system voltage is not interchangeable with another just because the plugs look alike.
sections.on_the_job: Check the nameplate voltage against the system in front of you — 120/240 single-phase, 208Y/120 and 480Y/277 three-phase are different worlds for device ratings even when the hardware looks similar.

sections.title: Conductors — general
sections.plain_explanation: Conductors in the Code are copper unless a rule or an equipment marking provides for another metal. Where other materials such as aluminum or copper-clad aluminum are used, the sizes in the Code's tables and rules are read in the column and on the terms for that material. The metal of the conductor is part of the design, not an afterthought at the supply house.
sections.on_the_job: Know which metal is on the spool before you size anything. Ampacity, terminations and the small-conductor limits all change with the metal.
sections.sharma_note: S-10: copper is Sharma's default. When CCA is used, size one AWG larger, use the aluminum column of Table 310.16, land it only on terminations listed for it, and never backstab.

sections.title: Conductor sizes — AWG and circular mils
sections.plain_explanation:
Conductor sizes are expressed in American Wire Gauge for the smaller sizes and in circular mil area for the larger ones. The size designation is a standard language: the same AWG number means the same conductor size whoever made the cable. Size by itself is not ampacity — the rating still comes from the ampacity tables, the termination limits and the conditions of use.

Circular-mil areas for the sizes Sharma pulls most (above 4/0, the kcmil number is the area in thousands of circular mils):
• 14 AWG — 4,110 circular mils
• 12 AWG — 6,530 circular mils
• 10 AWG — 10,380 circular mils
• 8 AWG — 16,510 circular mils
• 6 AWG — 26,240 circular mils
• 4 AWG — 41,740 circular mils
• 2 AWG — 66,360 circular mils
• 1/0 AWG — 105,600 circular mils
• 2/0 AWG — 133,100 circular mils
• 3/0 AWG — 167,800 circular mils
• 4/0 AWG — 211,600 circular mils
These areas are what the proportional upsizing rules work from — when conductors are upsized, grounding conductors are upsized by the ratio of these numbers (see 250.122 in Chapter 2).
sections.on_the_job: Speak sizes in AWG up through 4/0 and in kcmil above that, and never let a breaker handle rating substitute for the ampacity check behind it.

sections.title: Wiring integrity
sections.plain_explanation: Completed wiring installations must be free from short circuits, ground faults, and any connections to ground other than the ones the Code requires or permits — that is the whole rule of 110.7, and it is why continuity and insulation checks happen before energizing. Do not confuse it with equipment integrity: the rule that internal parts, busbars, wiring terminals, and other parts must not be damaged or contaminated lives at 110.12(B), not here.
sections.on_the_job: Before you energize, prove the install: no shorts, no ground faults, no stray grounds. If the gear itself is damaged or contaminated inside, that is a 110.12(B) problem — a different section, with the same stop-and-fix answer.

sections.title: Wiring methods — use only recognized methods
sections.plain_explanation:
Only wiring methods the Code recognizes for the application may be used. A cable or raceway that conducts electricity is not thereby a permitted wiring method for a given location: each method has its own article, its permitted uses and its prohibited uses, and those govern. Improvised assemblies and products used outside their article's limits fail here before any other rule is reached.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.8: A recognized wiring method is now clearly allowed in any premises wiring system, not just any building or occupancy, unless another rule limits it. That reaches wiring outside buildings too. A recognized wiring method can go in any type of building, occupancy or premises wiring system, unless another rule says otherwise.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Before running anything, name the method and its article — NM cable, EMT, PVC, MC and the rest each carry their own use lists. A method allowed indoors is not automatically allowed outdoors or in a wet location.

nec2023_change.change: A recognized wiring method is now clearly allowed in any premises wiring system, not just any building or occupancy, unless another rule limits it. That reaches wiring outside buildings too. A recognized wiring method can go in any type of building, occupancy or premises wiring system, unless another rule says otherwise.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 110.8 Recognized wiring methods

sections.title: Interrupting rating
sections.plain_explanation:
Equipment meant to interrupt current during a fault has to be able to interrupt the fault current that can actually be delivered at its terminals. A breaker asked to open a fault beyond its interrupting rating can fail violently instead of clearing the fault. The rating is printed on the device and must equal or exceed the available fault current at that point.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.9: A wording update using the defined term available fault current. Every breaker and fuse still has to be rated to interrupt the available fault current at its line terminals. Any breaker or fuse meant to open fault current needs an interrupting rating that meets or beats the available fault current at its line terminals.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Check the kAIC marking on breakers against the job's available fault current, especially close to large services and transformers. Series-rated combinations are only valid as tested and documented combinations, not as a field guess.

nec2023_change.change: A wording update using the defined term available fault current. Every breaker and fuse still has to be rated to interrupt the available fault current at its line terminals. Any breaker or fuse meant to open fault current needs an interrupting rating that meets or beats the available fault current at its line terminals.

sections.title: Circuit impedance and fault-current performance
sections.plain_explanation: The overcurrent devices, the total impedance of the circuit, and the other components have to work together so that, under a short circuit or ground fault, the fault is cleared without extensive damage to the equipment in the circuit. In practice this means a low-impedance fault path, correctly rated devices, and components whose short-circuit current ratings suit the system they are part of.
sections.on_the_job: This is the engineering reason behind tight bonding, correct conductor sizing and not mixing untested device combinations. A fault should be a breaker trip, not an equipment failure.

sections.title: Deteriorating agents
sections.plain_explanation: Equipment must not sit in conditions that will destroy it — dampness, corrosive gases or liquids, heat, mechanical damage and similar agents — unless it is identified for that environment. Ordinary equipment in a corrosive or wet environment fails early and can fail dangerously.
sections.on_the_job: Coastal Florida air, pool equipment rooms, fertilizer storage and car washes are the usual traps. Identify the environment first, then pick equipment identified for it.
sections.florida_note: Salt air along Florida coasts is a deteriorating agent. Exterior and coastal gear needs to be identified for the exposure, and corrosion found at service calls should be reported, not just wiped off.

sections.title: Mechanical execution of work — workmanship and unused openings
sections.plain_explanation:
Electrical work has to be done in a neat and workmanlike manner. Unused openings in enclosures, boxes and equipment have to be closed with closures that give protection much like the wall of the equipment itself — a missing knockout blank is an open door for fingers, pests and arc products. Conductors must also be protected where insulation can be damaged. (Keeping water out of enclosures in wet locations is a different rule — see 312.2 and 314.15 — not part of 110.12.) Part (B) covers integrity of equipment and connections: internal parts, busbars, wiring terminals, and other components must not be damaged or contaminated by foreign materials, and there must be no damaged, broken, bent, cut, or deteriorated parts.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.12: Neat and workmanlike is out. The standard for every electrical install is now professional and skillful work. The workmanship standard changed from neat and workmanlike to professional and skillful.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Close every unused opening with a listed blank or plug, not tape or a folded piece of can. Neat work is not cosmetic here — it is the section the inspector cites when a panel looks like a hazard even before testing anything.
sections.figure_idea: Before/after panel photos in drawing form: open knockouts and stray conductors on one side, blanks fitted and conductors dressed on the other.
sections.florida_note: Open knockouts in exterior Florida enclosures are also a pest and water entry. Close them the same day the gear is set.

nec2023_change.change: Neat and workmanlike is out. The standard for every electrical install is now professional and skillful work. The workmanship standard changed from neat and workmanlike to professional and skillful.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 110.12 Professional and skillful work

sections.title: Mounting and cooling of equipment
sections.plain_explanation: Equipment has to be firmly secured to its mounting surface, and it must not be mounted in a way that blocks the cooling it was designed for. Equipment that depends on air circulation cannot be buried in insulation or boxed in tight. Wooden plugs in masonry are not an acceptable way to secure equipment.
sections.on_the_job: Anchor gear with real fasteners into structure or masonry anchors, keep vents and fins clear, and check that a recessed installation still lets the equipment breathe as its instructions require.

sections.title: Electrical connections — terminations in general
sections.plain_explanation:
Most electrical failures start at a connection, and this section is the Code's main defense. Conductors must land on terminals suited to their metal and size, with the connection made by an approved method. Dissimilar metals in contact must be handled only where the device is identified for that combination, because corrosion between unlike metals loosens and overheats a joint over time. Solder, where used, cannot be the thing that holds a joint against pulling apart.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.14: Terminals now have to make a mechanically secure electrical connection, replacing the old thoroughly good wording, and the example metal pairs were cut from the dissimilar-metals rule. 110.14(A): landing a conductor on a terminal has to produce a mechanically secure electrical connection, with no damage to the wire.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: Read the lug and device markings before landing wire. CU-only means copper only. A connector for aluminum, copper and CCA together must carry the AL-CU or CU-AL marking, or the intermixed marking where the metals actually touch, and breaker and equipment lugs get the same check.
sections.sharma_note: S-10 CCA practice: 15A and 20A device screw terminals take copper and CCA unless marked otherwise; devices 30A and up are copper-only unless marked AL/CU. Copper and CCA are not dissimilar metals; aluminum with copper, or aluminum with CCA, is. Backstab (push-in) terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only — never backstab CCA, stranded wire, or 12 AWG. UNVERIFIED FLAG (v1 README item 9): the UL guide wording behind the CCA terminal markings (RTRT / WJQR / ZMVV / AALZ) was taken from NEMA and UL/IAEI quotations, not read first-hand in UL Product iQ, and no CC or CC/CU marking was found in the ZMVV table. Do not invent a marking. A NEMA citation to 404.15(C) for switch terminals was not checked against the code text and is not relied on here.
sections.figure_idea: Three lugs side by side marked CU, AL-CU and CU-AL, with a chart of which conductor metals each may take, and a crossed-out backstab terminal on CCA wire.

nec2023_change.change: Terminals now have to make a mechanically secure electrical connection, replacing the old thoroughly good wording, and the example metal pairs were cut from the dissimilar-metals rule. 110.14(A): landing a conductor on a terminal has to produce a mechanically secure electrical connection, with no damage to the wire.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 110.14 Terminal connections and dissimilar metals

sections.title: Temperature limits at terminations
sections.plain_explanation: A conductor's ampacity may be read from a higher temperature column only if the terminations at both ends are rated for that temperature. For circuits of 100A or less, or using 14 through 1 AWG conductors, the default is the 60 degree C column unless the equipment is marked otherwise. For larger circuits the default is the 75 degree C column. The temperature rating of a conductor cannot be used above the lowest temperature rating of any termination it lands on.
sections.on_the_job: This is why 90 degree wire still gets sized from the 60 or 75 degree column at the breaker. Read the breaker and equipment markings; existing v1 item L-033 works the 110.14(C)(1) case in detail.
sections.figure_idea: A conductor run drawn as a chain — wire rated 90, breaker lug rated 75, equipment lug rated 60 — with the whole chain sized at the weakest link, 60.

sections.title: Torque — tighten to the specified value
sections.plain_explanation: Where a manufacturer gives a torque value for a terminal, the connection has to be tightened to that value using a proper torque tool, unless the equipment has been tested and marked so another method is known to give the same result. Hand-tight by feel is not a value. The specified torque is normally printed on the equipment label or in its instructions.
sections.on_the_job: Keep a torque screwdriver and wrench on the truck, use the label value for every lug at trim and service work, and re-check after landing all conductors. Existing checklist item SP-15 covers the field routine.
sections.figure_idea: Torque screwdriver on a breaker lug with the panel label's torque table beside it.

sections.title: High-leg marking on 4-wire delta systems
sections.plain_explanation: On a 4-wire, 3-phase delta system, one phase conductor — the high leg — has a higher voltage to ground than the other two. That conductor has to be durably and permanently marked with an orange finish, or identified by other effective means, at the points the section specifies, such as where connections are made and where the grounded conductor is present. The marking is what keeps a 120V load from being landed on the leg that sits at 208V to ground.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma meets high legs on older light-commercial services. Before landing any 120V circuit in a delta panel, identify which leg is the high leg, confirm it is orange-marked, and keep 120V loads off it.
sections.figure_idea: A delta panel schedule with the B phase column shaded orange and the voltage-to-ground values 120 / 208 / 120 written under the three legs.

sections.title: Arc-flash hazard warning marking
sections.plain_explanation:
Certain equipment that is likely to be examined, adjusted or worked on while energized — such as switchboards, panelboards and motor control centers in other than dwelling settings — must carry a durable field-applied warning marking telling people about the arc-flash hazard. The marking warns; it does not replace safe work practice, and it belongs where a person approaching the gear will see it. 110.16(B) (NEC 2020): in other than dwelling units, service equipment rated 1200A or more also needs a permanent label (meeting 110.21(B)) showing the nominal system voltage, the available fault current at the service overcurrent devices, the clearing time of those devices based on that fault current, and the date the label was applied; it is not required where an arc-flash label is applied per acceptable industry practice.

NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 110.16(B): 110.16(B) now covers service equipment AND feeder-supplied equipment rated 1000A or more (was service equipment 1200A or more), and the permanent label must be an arc-flash label per applicable industry practice, with the date applied.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.on_the_job: On commercial work, confirm the arc-flash warning label is present and legible before final. Houses are not the target of this section, but the hazard it names is real on any energized panel.

nec2023_change.change: 110.16(B) now covers service equipment AND feeder-supplied equipment rated 1000A or more (was service equipment 1200A or more), and the permanent label must be an arc-flash label per applicable industry practice, with the date applied.
